title: Greening did not cause post-1997 runoff losses in 175 south-east Australian and 260 eastern US catchments: leaf area fell in 1997-2009 in Australia and explains at most one third after 2009
abstract: Question: after 1997, runoff in south-east Australia (SE-AU, 175 CAMELS-AUS catchments) and the eastern US (East-US, 260 CAMELS catchments) fell about 40 mm per year below each catchment's 1951-1996 rainfall-runoff relation. Earlier work excluded rain-gauge, evaporative-demand and storage causes. Did more leaf area (greening) cause these losses? Approach: we calculated catchment-mean LAI and NDVI for 1982-2022 from GIMMS LAI4g v1.2 (consolidated and AVHRR-only) and PKU GIMMS NDVI v1.2, removed the rain effect with a 1982-1996 fit, and compared the changes with runoff residuals. A plan written before any vegetation value fixed five endpoints. West-US and northern Australia were controls. Results: in 1997-2009, when SE-AU runoff was 24% below its relation, the rain-adjusted vegetation index was lower than in 1982-1996 in all three products (-0.9% to -2.6%). After 2009 SE-AU greened by 2-3%, which implies 5-29% of the loss. East-US LAI increased by 3-5%, which implies 19-35% of the offset, but NDVI did not increase. Control regions greened by similar amounts without a runoff loss. Catchment correlations between greening and loss were near zero with LAI and negative with NDVI. A 1997 step fit the regional runoff series better than the vegetation series in 5 of 6 cases and stayed after vegetation control. Victorian catchments burned in 1997-2009 did not lose more runoff. Exploratory: at equal aridity, more forested SE-AU catchments lost more runoff. Conclusion: satellite greening did not start the SE-AU loss and is not the main cause of either loss. Limitations: satellite indices do not see roots or stomata; products disagree in the East-US; sensor changes; a 15-year vegetation baseline; statistical sensitivities; some tests are post hoc.
